haberdasher.etymology: Prob. fr. Icel. hapurtask trumpery, trifles, perh. through French. It is possibly akin to E. haversack, and to Icel. taska trunk, chest, pocket, G. tasche pocket, and the orig. sense was perh., peddler's wares.

habergeon.etymology: F. haubergeon a small hauberk, dim. of OF. hauberc, F. haubert. See Hauberk.

habiliment.etymology: F. habillement, fr. habiller to dress, clothe, orig., to make fit, make ready, fr. habile apt, skillful, L. habilis. See Habile.

habilitate.etymology: LL. habilitatus, p. p. of habilitare to enable.

habit.etymology: OE. habit, abit fr. habit fr. L. habitus state, appearance, dress, fr. habere to have, be in a condition; prob. akin to E. have. See Have, and cf. Able, Binnacle, Debt, Due, Exhibit, Malady.

habitat.etymology: L., it dwells, fr. habitare. See Habit, v. t.

habitual.etymology: Cf. F. habituel, LL. habituals. See Habit, n.

habituate.etymology: L. habituatus, p. p. of habituare to bring into a condition or habit of body: cf. F. habituer. See Habit.

habitude.etymology: F., fr. L. habitudo condition. See Habit.

habitue.etymology: F., p. p. of habituer. See Habituate.

hachure.etymology: F., fr. hacher to hack. See Hatching.

hacienda.etymology: Sp., fr. OSp. facienda employment, estate, fr. L. facienda, pl. of faciendum what is to be done, fr. facere to do. See Fact.

hackamore.etymology: Cf. Sp. jaquima headstall of a halter.

hackney.etymology: OE. haceney, hacenay; cf. F. haquenée a pacing horse, an ambling nag, OF. also haquenée, Sp. hacanea, OSp. facanea, D. hakkenei, also OF. haque horse, Sp. haca, OSp. faca; perh akin to E. hack to cut, and orig. meaning, a jolting horse. Cf. Hack a horse, Nag.

haddock.etymology: OE. hadoc, haddok, of unknown origin; cf. Ir. codog, Gael. adag, F. hadot.

roots.meaning: An inseparable verbal prefix or particle. It is prefixed: (a) To verbs to express the contrary, and not the simple negative, of the action of the verb to which it is prefixed; as in uncoil, undo, unfold. (b) To nouns to form verbs expressing privation of the thing, quality, or state expressed by the noun, or separation from it; as in unchild, unsex. Sometimes particles and participial adjectives formed with this prefix coincide in form with compounds of the negative prefix un- (see 2d Un-); as in undone (from undo), meaning unfastened, ruined; and undone (from 2d un- and done) meaning not done, not finished. Un- is sometimes used with an intensive force merely; as in unloose.

hadj.etymology: Ar.hajj, fr. hajja to set out, walk, go on a pilgrimage.

hadrosaurus.etymology: NL., fr. Gr. "adro`s thick + say^ros lizard.

haft.etymology: AS. hæft; akin to D. & G. heft, Icel. hepti, and to E. Heave, or have. Cf. Heft.

hag.etymology: Scot. hag to cut; cf. E. hack.

hagbut.etymology: OF. haquebute, prob. a corruption of D. haakbus; haak hook + bus gun barrel. See Hook, and 2d Box, and cf. Arquebus.

haggada.etymology: Rabbinic haggadha, fr. Heb. higgidh to relate.

haggard.etymology: F. hagard; of German origin, and prop. meaning, of the hegde or woods, wild, untamed. See Hedge, 1st Haw, and -ard.

roots.meaning: The termination of many English words; as, coward, reynard, drunkard, mostly from the French, in which language this ending is of German origin, being orig. the same word as English hard. It usually has the sense of one who has to a high or excessive degree the quality expressed by the root; as, braggart, sluggard.

haggis.etymology: Scot. hag to hack, chop, E. hack. Formed, perhaps, in imitation of the F. hachis (E. hash), fr. hacher.

haggle.etymology: Freq. of Scot. hag, E. hack. See Hack to cut.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

haik.etymology: Ar. haik, fr. haka to weave.

hair.etymology: OE. her, heer, hær, AS. hær; akin to OFries, her, D. & G. haar, OHG. & Icel. har, Dan. haar, Sw. hår; cf. Lith. kasa.

halberd.etymology: F. hallebarde; of German origin; cf. MHG. helmbarte, G. hellebarte; prob. orig., an ax to split a helmet, fr. G. barte a broad ax (orig. from the same source as E. beard; cf. Icel. bar, a kind of ax, skegg beard, skeggia a kind of halberd) + helm helmet; but cf. also MNG. helm, halm, handle, and E. helve. See Beard, Helmet.

hale.etymology: Written also heil, Icel. heill; akin to E. whole. See Whole.

half.etymology: AS. healf, half, half; as a noun, half, side, part; akin to OS., OFries., & D. half, G. halb, Sw. half, Dan. halv, Icel. halfr, Goth. halbs. Cf. Halve, Behalf.

halibut.etymology: OE. hali holy + but, butte, flounder; akin to D. bot, G. butte; cf. D. heilbot, G. heilbutt. So named as being eaten on holidays. See Holy, Holiday.

hall.etymology: OE. halle, hal, AS. heal, heall; akin to D. hal, OS. & OHG. halla, G. halle, Icel. hölt, and prob. from a root meaning, to hide, conceal, cover. See Hell, Helmet.

halloo.etymology: Perh. fr. ah + lo; cf. AS. eala, G. halloh, F. haler to set (a dog) on. Cf. Hollo, interj.

hallow.etymology: OE. halowen, halwien, halgien, AS. halgian, fr. halig holy. See Holy.

hallucinate.etymology: L. hallucinatus, alucinatus, p. p. of hallucinari, alucinari, to wander in mind, talk idly, dream.

halo.etymology: L. halos, acc. halo, Gr. volvere, and E. voluble.

hals.etymology: AS. heals; akin to D., G., & Goth. hals. See Collar.

halt.etymology: Formerly alt, It. alto, G. halt, fr. halten to hold. See Hold.

halter.etymology: OE. halter, helter, helfter, AS. hælftre; akin to G. halfter, D. halfter, halster, and also to E. helve. See Helve.

ham.etymology: AS. ham; akin to D. ham, dial. G. hamme, OHG. hamma. Perh. named from the bend at the ham, and akin to E. chamber. Cf. Gammon ham.

hamadryad.etymology: L. Hamadryas, -adis, Gr. hamadryade. See Same, and Tree.

hame.etymology: Scot. haims, hammys, hems, OE. ham; cf. D. haam.

hamlet.etymology: OWE. hamelet, OF. hamelet, dim. of hamel, F. hameau, LL. hamellum, a dim. of German origin; cf. G. heim home. sq. root220. See Home.

hammer.etymology: OE. hamer, AS. hamer, hamor; akin to D. hamer, G. & Dan. hammer, Sw. hammare, Icel. hamarr, hammer, crag, and perh. to Gr. a stone.

hammock.etymology: A word of Indian origin: cf. Sp. hamaca. Columbus, in the Narrative of his first voyage, says: "A great many Indians in canoes came to the ship to-day for the purpose of bartering their cotton, and hamacas, or nets, in which they sleep."

hand.etymology: AS. hand, hond; akin to D., G., & Sw. hand, OHG. hant, Dan. haand, Icel. hönd, Goth. handus, and perh. to Goth. hinpan to seize (in comp.). Cf. Hunt.

handbook.etymology: Hand + book; cf. AS. handb, or G. handbuch.

handcuff.etymology: AS. handcops; hand hand + cosp, cops, fetter. The second part was confused with E. cuffs,

handicap.etymology: From hand in cap; -- perh. in reference to an old mode of setting a bargain by taking pieces of money from a cap.

handicraft.etymology: For handcraft, influenced by handiwork; AS. handcræft.

handiwork.etymology: OE. handiwerc, AS. handgeweorc; hand hand + geweorc work; prefix ge- + weorc. See Work.

roots.meaning: An Anglo-Saxon prefix. See Y-.

handle.etymology: OE. handlen, AS. handian; akin to D. handelen to trade, G. handeln. See Hand.

handsome.etymology: Hand + -some. It at first meant, dexterous; cf. D. handzaam dexterous, ready, limber, manageable, and E. handy.

roots.meaning: An adjective suffix having primarily the sense of like or same, and indicating a considerable degree of the thing or quality denoted in the first part of the compound; as in mettlesome, full of mettle or spirit; gladsome, full of gladness; winsome, blithesome, etc.

handy.etymology: OE. hendi, AS. hendig (in comp.), fr. hand hand; akin to D. handig, Goth. handugs clever, wise.

hang.etymology: OE. hangen, hangien, v. t. & i., AS. hangian, v. i., fr. h, v. t. (imp. heng, p. p. hongen); akin to OS. hang, v. i. D. hangen, v. t. & i., G. hangen, v. i, hängen, v. t, Isel hanga, v. i., Goth. hahan, v. t. (imp. haíhah), hahan, v. i. (imp. hahaida), and perh. to L. cunctari to delay. sq. root37.

hank.etymology: Cf. Dan. hank handle, Sw. hank a band or tie, Icel. hanki hasp, clasp, hönk, hangr, hank, coil, skein, G. henkel, henk, handle; ar prob. akin to E. hang. See Hang.

hanker.etymology: Prob. fr. hang; cf. D. hunkeren, hengelen.

hansom.etymology: From the name of the inventor.

happen.etymology: OE. happenen, hapnen. See Hap to happen.

happy.etymology: From Middle English happy ( “ fortunate, happy ” ) , perhaps an alteration of Middle English happyn , happen ( “ fortunate, happy ” ) , possibly related to or from Old Norse heppinn ( “ fortunate, happy ” ) ; and potentially assimilated to be equivalent to hap ( “ chance, luck, fortune ” ) +‎ -y . Compare also Icelandic heppinn ( “ lucky ” ) , Faroese heppin ( “ fortunate, lucky, happy ” ) , Norwegian Nynorsk heppen ( “ lucky ” ) , Scots happin ( “ fortunate, blessed ” ) . See further at hap .

harangue.etymology: F. harangue: cf. Sp. arenda, It. aringa; lit., a speech before a multitude or on the hustings, It. aringo arena, hustings, pulpit; all fr. OHG. hring ring, anything round, ring of people, G. ring. See Ring.

harass.etymology: F. harasser; cf. OF. harace a basket made of cords, harace, harasse,a very heavy and large shield; or harer to set (a dog) on.

harbinger.etymology: OE. herbergeour, OF. herbergeor one who provides lodging, fr. herbergier to provide lodging, F. héberger, OF. herberge lodging, inn, F. auberge; of German origin. See Harbor.

harbor.etymology: OE herbor, herberwe, herberge, Icel. herbergi (cf. OHG. heriberga), orig., a shelter for soldiers; herr army + bjarga to save, help, defend; akin to AS. here army, G. heer, OHG. heri, Goth. harjis, and AS. beorgan to save, shelter, defend, G. bergen. See Harry, 2d Bury, and cf. Harbinger.

hard.etymology: OE. heard, AS. heard; akin to OS. & D. heard, G. hart, OHG. harti, Icel. har, Dan. haard, Sw. hård, Goth. hardus, Gr.,, strength, and also to E. -ard, as in coward, drunkard, -crat, -cracy in autocrat, democracy; cf. Skr. kratu strength, to do, make. Gf.Hardy.

roots.meaning: The termination of many English words; as, coward, reynard, drunkard, mostly from the French, in which language this ending is of German origin, being orig. the same word as English hard. It usually has the sense of one who has to a high or excessive degree the quality expressed by the root; as, braggart, sluggard.
A termination denoting state, condition, quality, character, totality, as in manhood, childhood, knighthood, brotherhood. Sometimes it is written, chiefly in obsolete words, in the form - head.

hardy.etymology: F.hardi, p. p. fr. OF. hardir to make bold; of German origin, cf. OHG. hertan to harden, G. härten. See Hard, a.

harem.etymology: Ar.haram, orig., anything forbidden of sacred, fr. harama to forbid, prohibit.

harlequin.etymology: F. arlequin,formerly written also harlequin (cf. It, arlecchino), prob. fr. OF. hierlekin, hellequin, goblin, elf, which is prob. of German or Dutch origin; cf. D. hel hell. Cf. Hell, Kin.

harlot.etymology: OE.harlot, herlot, a vagabond, OF. harlot, herlot, arlot; cf. Pr. arlot, Sp. arlote, It. arlotto; of uncertain origin.

harm.etymology: OE.harm, hearm, AS.hearm; akin to OS. harm, G. harm grief, Icel. harmr, Dan. harme, Sw. harm; cf. OSlav. & Russ. sram' shame, Skr. crama toil, fatigue.

harmattan.etymology: F. harmattan, prob. of Arabic origin.

harmonic.etymology: L. harmonicus, Gr. harmonique. See Harmony.

harmonica.etymology: Fem. fr. L. harmonicus harmonic. See Harmonic, n.

harmonical.etymology: L. harmonicus, Gr. harmonique. See Harmony.

harness.etymology: OE. harneis, harnes, OF.harneis, F. harnais, harnois; of Celtic origin; cf. Armor. harnez old iron, armor, W. haiarn iron, Armor. houarn, Ir. iarann, Gael. iarunn. Gf. Iron.

harp.etymology: OE. harpe, AS. hearpe; akin to D. harp, G.harfe, OHG. harpha, Dan. harpe, Icel. & Sw. harpa.

harpoon.etymology: F. harpon, LL. harpo, perh. of Ger. origin, fr. the harp; cf. F. harper to take and grasp strongly, harpe a dog's claw, harpin boathook (the sense of hook coming from the shape of the harp); but cf. also Gr. harpy. Cf. Harp.

harpsichord.etymology: OF. harpechorde, in which the harpe is of German origin. See Harp, and Chord.

harpy.etymology: F. harpie, L. harpyia, Gr. Rapacious.

harridan.etymology: F. haridelle a worn-out horse, jade.

harrow.etymology: OE. harowen, harwen; cf. Dan. harve. See Harrow, n.

harry.etymology: OF. harwen, herien, her, AS. hergisn to act as an army, to ravage, plunder, fr. here army; akin to G. here army; akin to G. heer, Icel. herr, Goth. harjis, and Lith. karas war. Gf. Harbor, Herald, Heriot.

harsh.etymology: OE. harsk; akin to G. harsch, Dan. harsk rancid, Sw. härsk; from the same source as E. hard. See Hard, a.

hart.etymology: OE.hart, hert, heort, AS. heort, heorot; akin to D. hert, OHG. hiruz, hirz, G. hirsch, Icel. hjörtr, Dan. & Sw. hjort, L. cervus, and prob. to Gr.Horn.

harvest.etymology: OE. harvest, hervest, AS. hærfest autumn; akin to LG. harfst, D. herfst, OHG. herbist, G. herbst, and prob. to L. carpere to pluck, Gr. Carpet.

hash.etymology: Formerly hachey, hachee, F. hachis, hacher to hash; of German origin; cf. G. hippe sickle, OHG. hippa, for happia. Cf. Hatchet.

haslet.etymology: F. hâtelettes broil, for hastelettes, fr. F. haste spit; cf. L. hasta spear, and also OHG. harst gridiron.

hasp.etymology: OE. hasp, hesp, AS. hæpse; akin to G. haspe, häspe, Sw. & Dan. haspe, Icel. hespa.

hassock.etymology: Scot. hassock, hassik, a besom, anything bushy, a large, round turf used as a seat, OE. hassok sedgy ground, W. hesgog sedgy, hesg sedge, rushes; cf. Ir. seisg, and E. sedge.

hastate.etymology: L. hastatus, fr. hasta spear. Cf. Gad, n.

haste.etymology: OE. hast; akin to D. haast, G., Dan., Sw., & OFries. hast, cf. OF. haste, F. hâte (of German origin); all perh. fr. the root of E. hate in a earlier sense of, to pursue. See Hate.

hasty.etymology: Akin to D. haastig, G., Sw., & Dan. hastig. See Haste, n.

hat.etymology: AS. hæt, hætt; akin to Dan. hat, Sw. hatt, Icel. hattr a hat, höttr hood, D. hoed hat, G. hut, OHG. huot, and prob. to L. cassis helmet. Hood.

hatch.etymology: F. hacher to chop, hack. See Hash.

hatchel.etymology: OE. hechele, hekele; akin to D. hekel, G. hechel, Dan. hegle, Sw. häkla, and prob. to E. hook. See Hook, and cf. Hackle, Heckle.

hatchet.etymology: F. hachette, dim. of hache Hatch, Hash.

hate.etymology: OE. haten, hatien, AS. hatian; akin to OS. hatan, hat to be hostile to, D. haten to hate, OHG. hazz, hazz, G. hassen, Icel. & Sw. hata, Dan. hade, Goth. hatan, hatian. . Cf. Hate, n., Heinous.

hatred.etymology: OE. hatred, hatreden. See Hate, and cf. Kindred.

hatter.etymology: Prov. E., to entangle; cf. LG. verhaddern, verheddern, verhiddern.

hauberk.etymology: OF. hauberc, halberc, F.haubert, OHG. halsberc; hals neck + bergan to protect, G. bergen; akin to AS. healsbeorg, Icel. halsbjörg. See Collar, and Bury, v. t.

haughty.etymology: OE. hautein, F. hautain, fr. haut high, OF. also halt, fr. L. altus. See Altitude.

haul.etymology: OE. halen, halien, F. geholian to acquire, get, D. halen to fetch, pull, draw, OHG. hol, hal, G. holen, Dan. hale to haul, Sw. hala, and to L. calare to call, summon, Gr. Hale, v. t., Claim. Class, Council, Ecclesiastic.

haulm.etymology: OE. halm, AS. healm; akin to D., G., Dan., & Sw. halm, Icel. halmr, L. calamus reed, cane, stalk, Gr. Excel, Culminate, Culm, Shawm, Calamus.

haunch.etymology: F. hanche, of German origin; cf. OD. hancke, hencke, and also OHG. ancha; prob. not akin to E. ankle.

haunt.etymology: F. hanter; of uncertain origin, perh. from an assumed LL. ambitare to go about, fr. L. ambire (see Ambition); or cf. Icel. heimta to demand, regain, akin to heim home (see Home). sq. root36.

haustorium.etymology: LL., a well, fr. L. haurire, haustum, to drink.

hautboy.etymology: F. hautbois, lit., high wood; haut high + bois wood. So called on account of its high tone. See Haughty, Bush; and cf. Oboe.

hauteur.etymology: F., fr. haut high. See Haughty.

have.etymology: OE. haven, habben, AS. habben (imperf. hæfde, p. p. gehæfd); akin to OS. hebbian, D. hebben, OFries, hebba, OHG. hab, G. haben, Icel. hafa, Sw. hafva, Dan. have, Goth. haban, and prob. to L. habere, whence F. avoir. Cf. Able, Avoirdupois, Binnacle, Habit.

havelock.etymology: From Havelock, an English general distinguished in India in the rebellion of 1857.

haven.etymology: AS. hæfene; akin to D. & LG. haven, G. hafen, MNG. habe, Dan. havn, Icel. höfn, Sw. hamn; akin to E. have, and hence orig., a holder; or to heave (see Heave); or akin to AS. hæf sea, Icel. & Sw. haf, Dan. hav, which is perh. akin to E. heave.

haversack.etymology: F. havresac, G. habersack, sack for oats. See 2d Haver, and Sack a bag.

havoc.etymology: W. hafog devastation, havoc; or, if this be itself fr. E. havoc, cf. OE. havot, or AS. hafoc hawk, which is a cruel or rapacious bird, or F. hai, voux! a cry to hounds.

haw.etymology: OE. hawe, AS. haga; akin to D. haag headge, G. hag, hecke, Icel. hagi pasture, Sw. hage, Dan. have garden. Haggard, Ha- ha, Haugh, Hedge.

hawk.etymology: OE. hauk (prob. fr. Icel.), havek, AS. hafoc, heafoc; akin to D. havik, OHG. habuh, G. habicht, Icel. haukr, Sw. hök, Dan. hög, prob. from the root of E. heave.

hawse.etymology: Orig. a hawse hole, or hole in the ship; cf. Icel. hals, hals, neck, part of the bows of a ship, AS. heals neck. See Collar, and cf. Halse to embrace.

hawser.etymology: From F. hausser to hausserée towpath, towing, F. haussière hawser), LL. altiare, fr. L. altus high. See Haughty.

hawthorn.etymology: AS. hagaborn, hæg. See Haw a hedge, and Thorn.

hay.etymology: AS. hege: cf. F. haie, of German origin. See Haw a hedge, Hedge.

hazard.etymology: F. hazard, Sp. azar an unforeseen disaster or accident, an unfortunate card or throw at dice, prob. fr. Ar. zahr, zar, a die, which, with the article al the, would give azzahr, azzar.

haze.etymology: Cf. Icel. höss gray; akin to AS. hasu, heasu, gray; or Armor. aézen, ézen, warm vapor, exhalation, zephyr.

hazel.etymology: OE. hasel, AS. hæsel; akin to D. hazelaar, G. hazel, OHG. hasal, hasala, Icel. hasl, Dan & Sw. hassel, L. corylus, for cosylus.

head.etymology: OE. hed, heved, heaved, AS. heáfod; akin to D. hoofd, OHG. houbit, G. haupt, Icel. höfu, Sw. hufvud, Dan. hoved, Goth. haubip. The word does not corresponds regularly to L. caput head (cf. E. Chief, Cadet, Capital), and its origin is unknown.

headlong.etymology: OE. hedling, hevedlynge; prob. confused with E. long, a. & adv.

headquarters.etymology: but sometimes used as a n. sing.

health.etymology: OE. helthe, AS. hhal hale, sound, whole. See Whole.

heap.etymology: OE. heep, heap, heap, multitude, AS. heáp; akin to OS. h, D. hoop, OHG. houf, h, G. haufe, haufen, Sw. hop, Dan. hob., Icel. h troop, flock, Russ. kupa heap, crowd, Lith. kaupas. Cf. Hope, in Forlorn hope.

hear.etymology: OE. heren, AS,. hiéran, hran, hran; akin to OS. h, OFries. hera, hora, D. hooren, OHG. h, G. hören, Icel. heyra, Sw: höra, Dan. hore, Goth. hausjan, and perh. to Gr. acoustic. Cf. Hark, Hearken.

hearken.etymology: OE. hercnen, hercnien, AS. hercnian, heorcnian, fr. hiéran, h, to hear; akin to OD. harcken, horcken, LG. harken, horken, G. horchen. See Hear, and cf. Hark..

heart.etymology: OE. harte, herte, heorte, AS. heorte; akin to OS. herta, OFies. hirte, D. hart, OHG. herza, G. herz, Icel. hjarta, Sw. hjerta, Goth. haírt, Lith. szirdis, Russ. serdtse, Ir. cridhe, L. cor, Gr. Accord, Discord, Cordial, 4th Core, Courage.

hearth.etymology: OE. harthe, herth, herthe, AS. heor; akin to D. haard, heerd, Sw. härd, G. herd; cf. Goth. haúri a coal, Icel. hyrr embers, and L. cremare to burn.

heat.etymology: OE. hete, hæte, AS. h, h, fr. hat hot; akin to OHG. heizi heat, Dan. hede, Sw. hetta. See Hot.

heath.etymology: OE. heth waste land, the plant heath, AS. h; akin to D. & G. heide, Icel. hei waste land, Dan. hede, Sw. hed, Goth. haipi field, L. bucetum a cow pasture; cf. W. coed a wood, Skr. ksh field. sq. root20.

heathen.etymology: OE. hethen, AS. h, prop. an adj. fr. h heath, and orig., therefore, one who lives in the country or on the heaths and in the woods (cf. pagan, fr. pagus village); akin to OS. h, adj., D. heiden a heathen, G. heide, OHG. heidan, Icel. hei, adj., Sw. heden, Goth. haipn, n. fem. See Heath, and cf. Hoiden.

heave.etymology: OE. heven, hebben, As. hebban; akin to OS. hebbian, D. heffen, OHG. heffan, hevan, G. heven, Icel. häfva, Dan. hæve, Goth. hafjan, L. capere to take, seize; cf. Gr. Accept, Behoof, Capacious, Forceps, haft, Receipt.

heaven.etymology: OE. heven, hefen, heofen, AS. heofon; akin to OS. hevan, LG. heben, heven, Icel. hifinn; of uncertain origin, cf. D. hemel, G. himmel, Icel. himmin, Goth. himins; perh. akin to, or influenced by, the root of E. heave, or from a root signifying to cover, cf. Goth. gaham to put on, clothe one's self, G. hemd shirt, and perh. E. chemise.

heavy.etymology: OE. hevi, AS. hefig, fr. hebban to lift, heave; akin to OHG. hebig, hevig, Icel. höfigr, höfugr. See Heave.

hebdomad.etymology: L. hebdomas, -adis, Gr. "ebdoma`s the number seven days, fr. Seven.

hebdomadal.etymology: L. hebdomadalis, LL. hebdomadarius: cf. F. hebdomadaire.

hebdomadary.etymology: L. hebdomadalis, LL. hebdomadarius: cf. F. hebdomadaire.

hebraic.etymology: L. Hebraicus, Gr. hebraïque. See Hebrew.

hectare.etymology: F., fr. Gr. are an are.

hectic.etymology: F. hectique, Gr. sah to overpower, endure; cf. AS. sige, sigor, victory, G. sieg, Goth. sigis. Cf. Scheme.

hectogram.etymology: F. hectogramme, fr. Gr. gramme a gram.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying something written, a writing; also, a writer; as autograph, crystograph, telegraph, photograph.

hectoliter.etymology: F. hectolitre, fr. Gr. litre a liter.

hectolitre.etymology: F. hectolitre, fr. Gr. litre a liter.

hectometer.etymology: F. hectomètre, fr. Gr. mètre a meter.

hectometre.etymology: F. hectomètre, fr. Gr. mètre a meter.

hector.etymology: From the Trojan warrior Hector, the son of Priam.

hedge.etymology: OE. hegge, AS. hecg; akin to haga an inclosure, E. haw, AS. hege hedge, E. haybote, D. hegge, OHG. hegga, G. hecke. sq. root12. See Haw a hedge.

heed.etymology: OE. heden, AS. h; akin to OS. hdian, D. hoeden, Fries. hoda, OHG. huoten, G. hüten, Dan. hytte.Hood.

heel.etymology: OE. helden to lean, incline, AS. heldan, hyldan; akin to Icel. halla, Dan. helde, Sw. hälla to tilt, pour, and perh. to E. hill.

heft.etymology: From Heave: cf. hefe weight. Cf. Haft.

height.etymology: OE. heighte, heght, heighthe, AS. heáh, fr. heah high; akin to D. hoogte, Sw. höjd, Dan. höide, Icel. hæ, Goth. hauhipa. See High.

heinous.etymology: OF. haïnos hateful, F. haineux, fr. OF. haïne hate, F. haine, fr. haïr to hate; of German origin. See Hate.

heir.etymology: OE. heir, eir, hair, OF. heir, eir, F. hoir, L. heres; of uncertain origin. Cf. Hereditary, Heritage.

heirloom.etymology: Heir + loom, in its earlier sense of implement, tool. See Loom the frame.

heliocentric.etymology: Helio- + centric, centrical: cf. F. héliocentrique.

roots.meaning: A combining form from Gr. "h`lios the sun.
A combining form from Gr. "h`lios the sun.

A combining form from Gr. "h`lios the sun.
A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.

heliotrope.etymology: F. héliotrope, L. heliotropium, Gr. Heliacal, Trope.

roots.meaning: A combining form from Gr. "h`lios the sun.
A combining form signifying impressed form; stamp; print; type; typical form; representative; as in stereotype phototype, ferrotype, monotype.

helix.etymology: L. helix, Gr. volvere, and E. volute, voluble.

hell.etymology: AS. hell; akin to D. hel, OHG. hella, G. hölle, Icel. hal, Sw. helfvete, Dan. helvede, Goth. halja, and to AS. helan to conceal. Hele, v. t., Conceal, Cell, Helmet, Hole, Occult.

hellebore.etymology: L. helleborus, elleborus, Gr. hellébore, ellébore.

helm.etymology: OE. helme, AS. helma rudder; akin to D. & G. helm, Icel. hjalm, and perh. to E. helve.

helmet.etymology: OF. helmet, a dim of helme, F. heaume; of Teutonic origin; cf. G. helm, akin to AS. & OS. helm, D. helm, helmet, Icel. hjalmr, Sw. hjelm, Dan. hielm, Goth. hilms; and prob. from the root of AS. helan to hide, to hele; cf. also Lith. szalmas, Russ. shleme, Skr. çarman protection. sq. root17. Cf. Hele, Hell, Helm a helmet.

help.etymology: AS. helpan; akin to OS. helpan, D. helpen, G. helfen, OHG. helfan, Icel. hjalpa, Sw. hjelpa, Dan. hielpe, Goth. hilpan; cf. Lith. szelpti, and Skr. klp to be fitting.

helpmate.etymology: A corruption of the "help meet for him" of Genesis ii. 18.Fitzedward Hall.

helve.etymology: OE. helve, helfe, AS. hielf, helf, hylf, cf. OHG. halb; and also E. halter, helm of a rudder.

hem.etymology: OE., fr. AS. him, heom, dative pl. of. h he. See He, They.

hematite.etymology: L. haematites, Gr. a"i^ma, a"i`matos, blood.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.
Same as Hæma-.
A suffix used in medical terms to denote a morbid condition of some part, usually some kind of tumor; as in fibroma, glaucoma.
Same as Hæma-.

hemicrania.etymology: L.: cf. F. hémicrânie. See Cranium, and Megrim.

roots.meaning: A prefix signifying half.

hemisphere.etymology: L. hemisphaerium, Gr. hémisphère. See Hemi-, and Sphere.

roots.meaning: A prefix signifying half.

hemlock.etymology: OE. hemeluc, humloc, AS. hemlic, hymlic.

roots.meaning: Same as Hæma-, Hæmo-.
Same as Hæma-, Hæmo-.

hemp.etymology: OE. hemp, AS. henep, hænep; akin to D. hennep, OHG. hanaf, G. hanf, Icel. hampr, Dan. hamp, Sw. hampa, L. cannabis, cannabum, Gr. conoplia, Skr. a; all prob. borrowed from some other language at an early time. Cf. Cannabine, Canvas.

hen.etymology: AS. henn, hen, hæn; akin to D. hen, OHG. henna, G. henne, Icel. hna, Dan. höna; the fem. corresponding to AS. hana cock, D. haan, OHG. hano, G. hahn, Icel. hani, Dan. & Sw. hane. Prob. akin to L. canere to sing, and orig. meaning, a singer. Cf. Chanticleer.

hence.etymology: OE. hennes, hens (the s is prop. a genitive ending; cf. -wards), also hen, henne, hennen, heonnen, heonene, AS. heonan, heonon, heona, hine; akin to OHG. hinnan, G. hinnen, OHG. hina, G. hin; all from the root of E. he. See He.

roots.meaning: Suffixes denoting course or direction to; motion or tendency toward; as in backward, or backwards; toward, or towards, etc.

henchman.etymology: OE. hencheman, henxman; prob. fr. OE. & AS. hengest horse + E. man, and meaning, a groom. AS. hengest is akin to D. & G. hengst stallion, OHG. hengist horse, gelding.

henna.etymology: Ar. hinna alcanna (Lawsonia inermis or alba). Cf. Alcanna, Alkanet, Orchanet.

henry.etymology: From Joseph Henry, an American physicist.

hepatic.etymology: L. hepaticus, Gr. jecur, Skr. yak: cf. F. hépatique.

hepatica.etymology: NL. See Hepatic. So called in allusion to the shape of the lobed leaves or fronds.

roots.meaning: A suffix used in medical terms to denote an inflammatory disease of; as, arthritis; bronchitis, phrenitis.

heptad.etymology: L. heptas the number seven. Gr. "epta` seven.

herald.etymology: OE. herald, heraud, OF. heralt, heraut, herault, F. héraut, LL. heraldus, haraldus, fr. (assumed) OHG. heriwalto, hariwaldo, a (civil) officer who serves the army; hari, heri, army + waltan to manage, govern, G. walten; akin to E. wield. See Harry, Wield.

herb.etymology: OE. herbe, erbe, OF. herbe, erbe, F. herbe, L. herba; perh. akin to Gr. forbh` food, pasture, fe`rbein to feed.

herbarium.etymology: LL., fr. L. herba. See Herb, and cf. Arbor, Herbary.

herculean.etymology: L. herculeus, fr. Hercules: cf. F. herculéen. See Hercules.

herd.etymology: OE. herd, heord, AS. heord; akin to OHG. herta,G. herde, Icel. hjör, Sw. hjord, Dan. hiord, Goth. haírda; cf. Skr. çardha troop, host.

here.etymology: OE. here, hire, AS. heora, hyra, gen. pl. of he. See He.

hereditary.etymology: L. hereditarius, fr. hereditas heirship, inheritance, fr. heres heir: cf. F. héréditaire. See Heir.

heretic.etymology: L. haereticus, Gr. hérétique. See Heresy.

heritage.etymology: OE. heritage, eritage, OF. heritage, eritage, F. héritage, fr. hériter to inherit, LL. heriditare. See Hereditable.

heritor.etymology: Cf. LL. her, fr. L. heres an heir.

hermaphrodite.etymology: L. hermaphroditus, Gr. Hermaphroditus, son of Hermes and Aphrodite, when bathing, became joined in one body with Salmacis, the nymph of a fountain in Caria: cf. F. hermaphrodite.

hermetic.etymology: F. hermétique. See Note under Hermes, 1.

hermit.etymology: OE. ermite, eremite, heremit, heremite, F. hermite, ermite, L. eremita, Gr. Eremite.

hermitage.etymology: OE. hermitage, ermitage, F. hermitage, ermitage. See Hermit.

heroine.etymology: F. héroïne, L. heroina, Gr. Hero.

heron.etymology: OE. heiroun, heroun, heron, hern, OF. hairon, F. héron, OHG. heigir; cf. Icel. hegri, Dan. heire, Sw. häger, and also G. häher jay, jackdaw, OHG. hehara, higere, woodpecker, magpie, D. reiger heron, G. reiher, AS. hragra. Cf. Aigret, Egret.

herpetology.etymology: Written also, but less properly, erpetology.

herring.etymology: OE. hering, AS. hæring; akin to D. haring, G. häring, hering, OHG. haring, hering, and prob. to AS. here army, and so called because they commonly move in large numbers. Cf. Harry.

hesitant.etymology: L. haesitans, p. pr. of haesitare: cf. F. hésitant. See Hesitate.

hesitate.etymology: L. haesitatus, p. p. of haesitare, intens. fr. haerere to hesitate, stick fast; to hang or hold fast. Cf. Aghast, Gaze, Adhere.

hesperian.etymology: L. hesperius, fr. hesperus the evening star, Gr. Vesper.

roots.meaning: A combining form signifying other, other than usual, different; as, heteroclite, heterodox, heterogamous.
A combining form signifying other, other than usual, different; as, heteroclite, heterodox, heterogamous.

A combining form signifying other, other than usual, different; as, heteroclite, heterodox, heterogamous.

hew.etymology: AS. heáwan; akin to D. houwen, OHG. houwan, G. hauen, Icel. höggva, Sw. hugga, Dan. hugge, Lith. kova battle, Russ. kovate to hammer, forge. Cf. Hay cut grass, Hoe.

hexameter.etymology: L., fr. Gr. hexamètre. See Six, and Meter.

roots.meaning: A prefix or combining form, used to denote six, sixth, etc.; as, hexatomic, hexabasic.
A New Latin plural combining form or suffix from Gr. foot; as, hexapoda, myriapoda. See -pod.

heyday.etymology: Cf. G. heida, or hei da, D. hei daar. Cf. Hey, and There.

hiatus.etymology: L., fr. hiare, hiatum, to gape; akin to E. yawn. See Yawn.

hibernal.etymology: L. hibernalis, from the root of hiems winter; akin to Gr. hima cold, winter, snow: cf. F. hibernal.

hibernate.etymology: L. hibernare, hibernatum, fr. hibernu wintry. See Hibernal.

hiccough.etymology: OE. hickup, hicket, hickock; prob. of imitative origin; cf. D. & Dan. hik, Sw. hicka, Armor. hak, hik, W. ig, F. hoquet.

hickory.etymology: North American Indian pawcohiccora (Capt. J. Smith) a kind of milk or oily liquor pressed from pounded hickory nuts. "Pohickory" is named in a list of Virginia trees, in 1653, and this was finally shortened to "hickory." J. H. Trumbull.

hide.etymology: OE. hiden, huden, AS. h; akin to Gr. house, hut, and perh. to E. hide of an animal, and to hoard. Cf. Hoard.

hideous.etymology: OE. hidous, OF. hidous, hidos, hidus, hisdos, hisdous, F. hideux: cf. OF. hide, hisde, fright; of uncertain origin; cf. OHG. egidi horror, or L. hispidosus, for hispidus rough, bristly, E. hispid.

hie.etymology: OE. hien, hihen, highen, AS. higian to hasten, strive; cf. L. ciere to put in motion, call upon, rouse, Gr. cite.

hierarch.etymology: LL. hierarcha, Gr. ishiras vigorous, fresh, blooming) + hiérarque.

hierarchy.etymology: From Middle English ierarchie , jerarchie , from Old French ierarchie , jerarchie , from Late Latin ierarchia , from Latin hierarchia , from Ancient Greek ἱεραρχία ( hierarkhía , “ rule of a high priest ” ) , from ἱεράρχης ( hierárkhēs , “ high priest ” ) , from ἱερός ( hierós , “ holy ” ) + ἄρχω ( árkhō , “ to rule ” ) , equivalent to hiero- +‎ -archy . The H was re-added c. 1500 due to influence from Classical Latin.

hieroglyph.etymology: Cf. F. hiéroglyphe. See Hieroglyphic, a.

hieroglyphic.etymology: Cf. F. hiéroglyphe. See Hieroglyphic, a.

hilarity.etymology: L. hilaritas: cf. F. hilarité. See Hilarious.

hill.etymology: OE. hil, hul, AS. hyll; akin to OD. hille, hil, L. collis, and prob. to E. haulm, holm, and column. Cf. 2d Holm.

hilt.etymology: AS. hilt, hilte; akin to OHG. helza, Prov. G. hilze, Icel. hjalt.

himalayan.etymology: Skr. himalaya, prop., the abode of snow.

hind.etymology: OE. hine, AS. hine, hina, orig. gen. pl. of hiwan domestics; akin to Icel. hju man and wife, domestics, family, Goth. heiwafrauja master of the house, G. heirath marriage; cf. L. civis citizen, E. city or E. home. Cf. Hide a measure of land.

hinder.etymology: OE. hindere, AS. hinder, adv., behind; akin to OHG. hintar, prep., behind, G. hinter, Goth. hindar; orig. a comparative, and akin to AS. hine hence. See Hence, He, and cf. Hind, a., Hindmost.

hindermost.etymology: The superlative of hind. See Hind, a.

hindi.etymology: Prop. a Per. adj. meaning, Indian, Hindoo.

hindmost.etymology: The superlative of hind. See Hind, a.

hindoo.etymology: Per. Hindu, fr. Hind, Hindustan, India. Cf. Indian.

hindu.etymology: Per. Hindu, fr. Hind, Hindustan, India. Cf. Indian.

hindustani.etymology: Hind. Hindustani an Indian, fr. Hind. and Per. Hindustan India.

hinge.etymology: OE. henge, heeng; akin to D. heng, LG. henge, Prov. E. hingle a small hinge; connected with hang, v., and Icel. hengja to hang. See Hang.

hint.etymology: OE. henten, hinten, to seize, to catch, AS. hentan to pursue, take, seize; or Icel. ymta to mutter, ymtr a muttering, Dan. ymte to whisper. sq. root36. Cf. Hent.

hip.etymology: OE. hipe, huppe, AS. hype; akin to D. heup, OHG. huf, G. hüfte, Dan. hofte, Sw. höft, Goth. hups; cf. Icel. huppr, and also Gr. kumpis ham.

hircine.etymology: L. hircinus, fr. hircus hegoat: cf. F. hircin.

hire.etymology: OE. hire, hure, AS. h; akin to D.huur, G. heuer, Dan. hyre, Sw. hyra.

hireling.etymology: AS. h. See Hire, n., and -ling.

roots.meaning: A noun suffix, commonly having a diminutive or a depreciatory force; as in duck-ling, dosling, hireling, fosterling, firstling, underling.

hirsute.etymology: L. hirsutus; prob. akin to horridus horrid. Cf. Horrid.

hirudinea.etymology: NL., fr. L. hirudo, hirudinis, a leech.

hiss.etymology: AS. hysian; prob. of imitative originhissen, OD. hisschen.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

historic.etymology: L. historicus, Gr. historique. See History.

historical.etymology: L. historicus, Gr. historique. See History.

history.etymology: L.historia, Gr. 'istori`a history, information, inquiry, fr. 'istwr, "istwr, knowing, learned, from the root of wit. See Wit, and cf. Story.

histrionic.etymology: L. histrionicus: cf. F. histronique. See Histrion.

hit.etymology: OE. hitten, hutten, of Scand. origin; cf. Dan. hitte to hit, find, Sw. & Icel. hitta.

hitch.etymology: Cf. Scot. hitch a motion by a jerk, and hatch, hotch, to move by jerks, also Prov. G. hiksen, G. hinken, to limp, hobble; or E. hiccough; or possibly akin to E. hook.

hither.etymology: OE. hider, AS. hider; akin to Icel. hra, Dan. hid, Sw. hit, Goth. hidrcitra on this side, or E. here, he. He.

hives.etymology: Scot.; perh. akin to E. heave.

hoar.etymology: OE. hor, har, AS. har; akin to Icel. harr, and to OHG. her illustrious, magnificent; cf. Icel. Heiedh brightness of the sky, Goth. hais torch, Skr. ketus light, torch. Cf. Hoary.

hoard.etymology: OE. hord, AS. hord; akin to OS. hord, G. hort, Icel. hodd, Goth. huzd; prob. from the root of E. hide to conceal, and of L. custos guard, E. custody. See Hide to conceal.

hoarding.etymology: From OF. hourd, hourt, barrier, palisade, of German or Dutch origin; cf. D. horde hurdle, fence, G. horde, hürde; akin to E. hurdle. sq. root16. See Hurdle.

hoarse.etymology: OE. hors, also hos, has, AS. has; akin to D. heesch, G. heiser, Icel. hass, Dan. hæs, Sw. hes. Cf. Prov. E. heazy.

hoax.etymology: Prob. contr. fr. hocus, in hocus-pocus.

hob.etymology: Prob. akin to hump. Cf. Hub.

hobble.etymology: OE. hobelen, hoblen, freq. of hoppen to hop; akin to D. hobbelen, hoblen, hoppeln. See Hop to jump, and cf. Hopple

hobbledehoy.etymology: Cf. Prob. E. hobbledygee with a limping movement; also F. hobereau, a country squire, E. hobby, and OF. hoi to-day; perh. the orig. sense was, an upstart of to-day.

hobbler.etymology: OE. also hobeler, OF. hobelier, LL. hobellarius. See Hobby a horse.

hobby.etymology: OE. hobi; cf. OF. hobe, hobé, F. hobereau a hobby, a species of falcon. OF. hober to move, stir. Cf. Hobby a horse.

hobbyhorse.etymology: OE. hobin a nag, OF. hobin hobby; cf. hober to stir, move; prob. of German or Scand. origin; cf. Dan. hoppe a mare, dial. Sw. hoppa; perh. akin to E. hop to jump.

hobnob.etymology: AS. habban to have + habban to have not; ne not + habban to have. See Have, and cf. Habnab.

hock.etymology: So called from Hochheim, in Germany.

hod.etymology: Prov. E. for hold, i. e., that which holds. See Hold.

hoe.etymology: OF. hoe, F. houe; of German origin, cf. OHG. houwa, howa, G. haue, fr. OHG. houwan to hew. See Hew to cut.

hog.etymology: Prob. akin to E. hack to cut, and meaning orig., a castrated boar; cf. also W. hwch swine, sow, Armor. houc'h, hoc'h. Cf. Haggis, Hogget, and Hoggerel.

hogshead.etymology: D. okshoofd; akin to Sw. oxhufvud, Dan. oxehoved, G. oxhoft; apparently meaning orig., ox head, but it is not known why this name was given. Cf. Ox, Head.

hoist.etymology: OE. hoise, hyse, OD. hyssen, D. hijshen; akin to LG. hissen, Dan. hisse, Sw. hissa.

hold.etymology: D. hol hole, hollow. See Hole.

hole.etymology: OE. hol, hole, AS. hol, hole, cavern, from hol, a., hollow; akin to D. hol, OHG. hol, G. hohl, Dan.huul hollow, hul hole, Sw. hål, Icel. hola; prob. from the root of AS. helan to conceal. See Hele, Hell, and cf. Hold of a ship.

holla.etymology: F. hola; ho ho + là there, fr. L. illac that way, there. Cf. Hollo.

hollandaise.etymology: F. hollandaise, fem. of hollandais Dutch.

hollow.etymology: OE. holow, holgh, holf, AS. holh a hollow, hole. Cf. Hole.

holly.etymology: OE holi, holin, AS. holen, holegn; akin to D. & G. hulst, OHG. huls hulis, W. celyn, Armor. kelen, Gael. cuilionn, Ir. cuileann. Cf. 1st Holm, Hulver.

hollyhock.etymology: OE. holihoc; holi holy + hoc mallow, AS. hoc; cf. W. hocys mallows, hocys bendigaid hollyhock, lit., blessed mallow. Prob. so named because brought from the Holy Land. See Holy.

holocaust.etymology: L. holocaustum, Gr. "o'los whole + kaysto`s burnt, fr. kai`ein to burn (cf. Caustic): cf. F. holocauste.

holograph.etymology: L.holographus entirely autograph, Gr. "olo`grafos; "o`los whole + gra`fein to write: cf. F. holographe, olographe.

roots.meaning: A combining form fr. Gr. "o`los whole.

holster.etymology: D. holster; skin to AS. heolstor den, cave, fr.helan to conceal, and to Icel. hulstr case, Goth.hulistr covering, veil, huljan to cover. sq. root17. See Hele to cover, Hell, and cf. Housing, Houss.

holy.etymology: OE. holi, hali, AS.halig, fr. hæl health, salvation, happiness, fr. hal whole, well; akin to OS. h, D. & G.heilig, OHG. heilac, Dan. hellig, Sw. helig, Icel. heilagr. See Whole, and cf. Halibut, Halidom, Hallow, Hollyhock.

homage.etymology: OF.homage, homenage, F. hommage, LL. hominaticum, homenaticum, from L. homo a man, LL. also, a client, servant, vassal; akin to L. humus earth, Gr.groom in bridegroom. Cf. Bridegroom, Human.

homicide.etymology: F., fr. L. homicidium, fr. homicida a man slayer; homo man + caedere to cut, kill. See Homage, and cf. Concise, Shed, v. t.

homily.etymology: LL. homilia, Gr. homélie. See Same.

hominy.etymology: From North American Indian auhúminea parched corn.

homogeneous.etymology: Gr. homogène. See Same, and Kin.

homograph.etymology: Gr. "omo`grafos with the same letters; "omo`s the same + gra`fein to write.

roots.meaning: A combining form from Gr. "omo`s, one and the same, common, joint.

honest.etymology: OE. honest, onest, OF. honeste, oneste, F. honnête, L. honestus, fr. honos, honor, honor. See Honor.

honesty.etymology: OE. honeste, oneste, honor, OF. honesté, onesté (cf. F. honnêteté), L. honestas. See Honest, a.

honey.etymology: OE. honi, huni, AS. hunig; akin to OS. honeg, D. & G. honig, OHG. honag, honang, Icel. hunang, Sw. håning, Dan. honning, cf. Gr. kaa grain.

honeycomb.etymology: AS. hunigcamb. See Honey, and 1st Comb.

honeysuckle.etymology: Cf. AS. hunis privet. See Honey, and Suck.

honor.etymology: OE. honor, honour, onour, onur, OF. honor, onor, honur, onur, honour, onour, F. honneur, fr. L. honor, honos.

honorarium.etymology: L. honorarium (sc. donum), fr. honorarius. See Honorary, a.

honorary.etymology: L. honorarium (sc. donum), fr. honorarius. See Honorary, a.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

A suffix, denoting that the element indicated enters into certain compounds with its highest valence, or with a valence relatively higher than in compounds where the name of the element ends in -ous; as, ferric, sulphuric. It is also used in the general sense of pertaining to; as, hydric, sodic, calcic.

hood.etymology: OE. hood, hod, AS. hod; akin to D. hoed hat, G. hut, OHG. huot, also to E. hat, and prob. to E. heed. sq. root13.

hoof.etymology: OE. hof, AS. hof; akin to D. hoef, G1huf, OHG. huof, Icel. hofr, Sw. hof, Dan. hov; cf. Russ. kopuito, Skr. çapha. sq. root225.

hook.etymology: OE. hok, AS. hoc; cf. D. haak, G. hake, haken, OHG. hako, hago, haggo, Icel. haki, Sw. hake, Dan. hage. Cf. Arquebuse, Hagbut, Hake, Hatch a half door, Heckle.

hookah.etymology: Per. or Ar. huqqa a round box or casket, a bottle through which the fumes pass when smoking tobacco.

hoop.etymology: OE. hope; akin to D. hoep, hoepel.

hoopoe.etymology: So called from its cry; cf. L. upupa, Gr. hop, F. huppe; cf. also G. wiedenhopf, OHG. wituhopfo, lit., wood hopper.

hoopoo.etymology: So called from its cry; cf. L. upupa, Gr. hop, F. huppe; cf. also G. wiedenhopf, OHG. wituhopfo, lit., wood hopper.

hoot.etymology: OE. hoten, houten, huten; cf. OSw. huta, Sw. huta ut to take one up sharply, fr. Sw. hut interj., begone! cf. also W. hwt off! off with it! away! hoot!

hop.etymology: OE. hoppen to hop, leap, dance, AS. hoppian; akin to Icel. & Sw. hoppa, Dan. hoppe, D. huppelen, G. hüpfen.

hope.etymology: Cf. Icel. hop a small bay or inlet.

horary.etymology: LL. horarius, fr. L. hora hour: cf. F. horaire. See Hour.

horde.etymology: F. horde (cf. G. horde), fr. Turk. ord, ordi, camp; of Tartar origin.

hordeolum.etymology: NL., fr. L. hordeolus, dim. of hordeum barley.

horehound.etymology: OE. horehune, AS. harhune; har hoar, gray + hune horehound; cf. L. cunila a species of organum, GR. kn to smell.

horn.etymology: AS. horn; akin to D. horen, hoorn, G., Icel., Sw., & Dan. horn, Goth. haúrn, W., Gael., & Ir. corn, L. cornu, Gr. cheer, cranium, cerebral; cf. Skr. çiras head. Cf. Carat, Corn on the foot, Cornea, Corner, Cornet, Cornucopia, Hart.

hornblende.etymology: G., fr. horn horn + blende blende.

hornet.etymology: AS. hyrnet; akin to OHG. hornaz, hornuz, G. horniss; perh. akin to E. horn, and named from the sound it makes as if blowing the horn; but more prob. akin to D. horzel, Lith. szirszone, L. crabo.

horologe.etymology: OE. horologe, orloge, timepiece, OF. horloge, orloge, oriloge, F. horloge, L. horologium, fr. Gr. Hour, and Logic.

horoscope.etymology: F. horoscope, L. horoscopus, fr. Gr. n., a horoscope; Hour, and -scope.

roots.meaning: A combining form usually signifying an instrument for viewing (with the eye) or observing (in any way); as in microscope, telescope, altoscope, anemoscope.

horrible.etymology: OE. horrible, orrible, OF. horrible, orrible, F. horrible, fr. L. horribilis, fr. horrere. See Horror.

horrid.etymology: L. horridus. See Horror, and cf. Ordure.

horrific.etymology: L. horrifieus; horrere to be horrible + -ficare (in comp.) to make: cf. F. horrifique. See Horror, -fy.

horripilation.etymology: L. horripilatio, fr. horripilare to bristle; horrere to bristle + pilus the hair: cf. F. horripilation.

horse.etymology: AS. hors; akin to OS. hros, D. & OHG. ros, G. ross, Icel. hross; and perh. to L. currere to run, E. course, current Cf. Walrus.

horticulture.etymology: L. hortus garden + cultura culture: cf. F. horticulture. See Yard an inclosure, and Culture.

hosanna.etymology: Gr. hoshi'ah nnasave now, save, we pray, hoshia' to save (Hiphil, a causative form, of yasha') + na, a particle.

hose.etymology: AS. hose; akin to D. hoos, G. hose breeches, OHG. hosa, Icel. hosa stocking, gather, Dan. hose stocking; cf. Russ. koshulia a fur jacket.

hospice.etymology: F., fr. L. hospitium hospitality, a place where strangers are entertained, fr. hospes stranger, guest. See Host a landlord.

hospitable.etymology: Cf. OF. hospitable, LL. hospitare to receive as a guest. See Host a landlord.

hospital.etymology: OF. hospital, ospital, F. hôpital, LL. hospitale (or perh. E. hospital is directly from the Late Latin), from L. hospitalis relating to a guest, hospitalia apartments for guests, fr. hospes guest. See Host a landlord, and cf. Hostel, Hotel, Spital.

host.etymology: LL. hostia sacrifice, victim, from hostire to strike.

hostage.etymology: OE. hostage, OF. hostage, ostage, F. ôtage, LL. hostaticus, ostaticum, for hospitaticum, fr. L. hospes guest, host. The first meaning is, the state of a guest, hospitality; hence, the state of a hostage (treated as a guest); and both these meanings occur in Old French. See Host a landlord.

hostel.etymology: OE. hostel, ostel, OF. hostel, ostel, LL. hospitale, hospitalis, fr. L. hospitalis. See Hospital, and cf. Hotel.

hostelry.etymology: OE. hostelrie, hostelrye, ostelrie, OF. hostelerie, fr. hostel. See Hostel.

hostess.etymology: OE. hostesse, ostesse. See Host a landlord.

hostile.etymology: L. hostilis, from hostis enemy: cf. F. hostile. See Host an army.

hostler.etymology: OE. hosteler, osteler, innkeeper, OF. hostelier, F. hôtelier. See Hostel, and cf. Hospitaler, Hosteler.

hot.etymology: OE. hot, hat, AS. hat; akin to OS. het, D. heet, OHG. heiz, G. heiss, Icel. heitr, Sw. het, Dan. heed, hed; cf. Goth. heito fever, hais torch. Cf. Heat.

hotchpotch.etymology: F. hochepot, fr. hocher to shake + pot pot; both of Dutch or German origin; cf. OD. hutspot hotchpotch, D. hotsen, hutsen, to shake. See Hustle, and Pot, and cf. Hodgepodge.

hotel.etymology: F. hôtel, OF. hostel. See Hostel.

hottentot.etymology: D. Hottentot; -- so called from hot and tot, two syllables of frequent occurrence in their language. Wedgwood.

hound.etymology: OE. hound, hund, dog, AS. hund; akin to OS. & OFries. hund, D. hond, G. hund, OHG. hunt, Icel. hundr, Dan. & Sw. hund, Goth. hunds, and prob. to Lith. sz, Ir. & Gael. cu, L. canis, Gr. çvan. sq. root229. Cf. Canine, Cynic, Kennel.

hour.etymology: OE. hour, our, hore, ure, OF. hore, ore, ure, F. heure, L. hora, fr. Gr. Year, and cf. Horologe, Horoscope.

houri.etymology: Per. huri, hura, hur; akin to Ar. hur, pl. of ahwar beautiful-eyed, black-eyed.

hours.etymology: A translation of L. Horae (Gr. Hour.

house.etymology: OE. hous, hus, AS. h; akin to OS. & OFries. h, D. huis, OHG. h, G. haus, Icel. h, Sw. hus, Dan. huus, Goth. gudh, house of God, temple; and prob. to E. hide to conceal. See Hide, and cf. Hoard, Husband, Hussy, Husting.

housing.etymology: From House. In some of its senses this word has been confused with the following word.

hovel.etymology: OE. hovel, hovil, prob. a dim. fr. AS. hof house; akin to D. & G. hof court, yard, Icel. hof temple; cf. Prov. E. hove to take shelter, heuf shelter, home.

howdy.etymology: Scot., also houdy- wife. Of uncertain origin; cf. OSw. jordgumma; or perh. fr. E. how d'ye.

howitzer.etymology: G. haubitze, formerly hauffnitz, Bohem. haufnice, orig., a sling.

howl.etymology: OE. houlen, hulen; akin to D. huilen, MHG. hiulen, hiuweln, OHG. hiuwilon to exult, h owl, Dan. hyle to howl.

hubbub.etymology: Cf. Whoobub, Whoop, Hoop, v. i.

huck.etymology: See Hawk to offer for sale, Huckster.

huckaback.etymology: Perh. orig., peddler's wares; cf. LG. hukkebak pickback. Cf. Huckster.

huckster.etymology: OE. hukstere, hukster, OD. heukster, D. heuker; akin to D. huiken to stoop, bend, OD. huycken, huken, G. hocken, to squat, Icel. h; -- the peddler being named from his stooping under the load on his back. Cf. Hawk to offer for sale.

huddle.etymology: Cf. OE. hoderen, hodren, to cover, keep, warm; perh. akin to OE. huden, hiden, to hide, E. hide, and orig. meaning, to get together for protection in a safe place. Cf. Hide to conceal.

hue.etymology: OE. hew, heow, color, shape, form, AS. hiw, heow; akin to Sw. hy skin, complexion, Goth. hiwi form, appearance.

huff.etymology: Cf. OE. hoove to puff up, blow; prob. of imitative origin.

hug.etymology: Prob. of Scand. origin; cf. Dan. sidde paa huk to squat, Sw. huka sig to squat, Icel. h. Cf. Huckster.

huge.etymology: OE. huge, hoge, OF. ahuge, ahoge.

huguenot.etymology: F., properly a dim. of Hugues. The name is probably derived from the Christian name (Huguenot) of some person conspicuous as a reformer.

hulk.etymology: OE. hulke a heavy ship, AS. hulc a light, swift ship; akin to D. hulk a ship of burden, G. holk, OHG. holcho; perh. fr. LL. holcas, Gr. Wolf, Holcad.

hull.etymology: OE. hul, hol, shell, husk, AS. hulu; akin to G. hülle covering, husk, case, hüllen to cover, Goth. huljan to cover, AS. helan to hele, conceal. sq. root17. See Hele, v. t., Hell.

hum.etymology: Of imitative origin; cf. G. hummen, D. hommelen. sq. root15.

human.etymology: L. humanus; akin to homo man: cf. F. humain. See Homage, and cf. Humane, Omber.

humane.etymology: L. humanus: cf. F. humain. See Human.

humanity.etymology: L. humanitas: cf. F. humanité. See Human.

humble.etymology: F., fr. L. humilis on the ground, low, fr. humus the earth, ground. See Homage, and cf. Chameleon, Humiliate.

humblebee.etymology: OE. humbilbee, hombulbe; cf. D. hommel, G. hummel, OHG. humbal, Dan. humle, Sw. humla; perh. akin to hum. sq. root15. Cf. Bumblebee.

humbug.etymology: Prob. fr. hum to impose on, deceive + bug a frightful object.

humic.etymology: L. humus the earth, ground: cf. F. humique.

humid.etymology: L. humidus, umidus, fr. humere, umere, to be moist; akin to uvidus moist, Gr. uksh to wet, sprinkle, and Icel. vökr moist, and perh. to E. ox: cf. F. humide.

humiliate.etymology: L. humiliatus, p.p. of humiliare. See Humble.

humility.etymology: OE. humilite, OF. humilité, humelité, F. humilité, fr. L. humiliatis. See Humble.

hummock.etymology: Prob. a dim. of hump. See Hump.

humor.etymology: OE. humour, OF. humor, umor, F. humeur, L. humor, umor, moisture, fluid, fr. humere, umere, to be moist. See Humid.

humorous.etymology: Cf. L. humorosus, umorosus, moist. See Humor.

hump.etymology: Cf. D. homp a lump, LG. hump heap, hill, stump, possibly akin to E. heap. Cf. Hunch.

humulin.etymology: NL. Humulus, the genus including the hop.

hun.etymology: L. Hunni, also Chunni, and Chuni; cf. AS. H, H, OHG. H, G. Hunnen.

hunch.etymology: Perh. akin to huckle; cf. hump, hunch, bunch, hunk.

hundred.etymology: OE. hundred, AS. hundred a territorial division; hund hundred + a word akin to Goth. ga-ra to count, L. ratio reckoning, account; akin to OS. hunderod, hund, D. hondred, G. hundert, OHG. also hunt, Icel. hundra, Dan. hundrede, Sw. hundra, hundrade, Goth. hund, Lith. szimtas, Russ. sto, W. cant, Ir. cead, L. centum, Gr. çata. sq. root309. Cf. Cent, Century, Hecatomb, Quintal, and Reason.

hunger.etymology: AS. hungor; akin to OFries. hunger, D. honger, OS. & OHG. hungar, G. hunger, Icel. hungr, Sw. & Dan. hunger, Goth. h hunger, huggrjan to hunger.

hunt.etymology: AS. huntian to hunt; cf. hentan to follow, pursue, Goth. hin (in comp.) to seize. sq. root36. Cf. Hent.

hurdle.etymology: OE. hurdel, hirdel, AS. hyrdel; akin to D. horde, OHG. hurt, G. hürde a hurdle, fold, pen, Icel. hur door, Goth. haúrds, L. cratis wickerwork, hurdle, Gr. k to spin, c to bind, connect. sq. root16. Cf. Crate, Grate, n.

hurl.etymology: OE. hurlen, hourlen; prob. contracted fr. OE. hurtlen to hurtle, or probably akin to E. whirl. sq. root16. See Hurtle.

hurrah.etymology: Cf. G., Dan., & Sw. hurra. Cf. Huzza.

hurricane.etymology: Sp. hurracan; orig. a Carib word signifying, a high wind.

hurry.etymology: OE. horien; cf. OSw. hurra to whirl round, dial. Sw. hurr great haste, Dan. hurre to buzz, Icel. hurr hurly-burly, MHG. hurren to hurry, and E. hurr, whir to hurry; all prob. of imitative origin.

hurt.etymology: OE. hurten, hirten, horten, herten; prob. fr. OF. hurter, heurter, to knock, thrust, strike, F. heurter; cf. W. hyrddu to push, drive, assault, hwrdd a stroke, blow, push; also, a ram, the orig. sense of the verb thus perhaps being, to butt as a ram; cf. D. horten to push, strike, MHG. hurten, both prob. fr. Old French.

hurtle.etymology: OE. hurtlen, freq. of hurten. See Hurt, v. t., and cf. Hurl.

husband.etymology: OE. hosebonde, husbonde, a husband, the master of the house or family, AS. h master of the house; h house + bunda, bonda, householder, husband; prob. fr. Icel. h house master, husband; h house + b dwelling, inhabiting, p.pr. of b to dwell; akin to AS. b, Goth. bauan. See House Be, and cf. Bond a slave, Boor.

hush.etymology: OE. huschen, hussen, prob. of imitative origin; cf. LG. hussen to lull to sleep, G. husch quick, make haste, be silent.

husk.etymology: Prob. for hulsk, and from the same root as hull a husk. See Hull a husk.

hussar.etymology: Hung. huszár, from husz twenty, because under King Matthais I., in the fifteenth century, every twenty houses were to furnish one horse soldier; cf. G. husar, F. houssard, hussard, from the same source.

hustings.etymology: OE. husting an assembly, coucil, AS. h; of Scand. origin; cf. Icel. h; h home + thing, assembly, meeting; akin to Dan. & Sw. ting, E. thing. See House, and Thing.

hustle.etymology: D. hustelen to shake, fr. husten to shake. Cf. Hotchpotch.

hut.etymology: OE. hotte; akin to D. hut, G. hütte, OHG. hutta, Dan. hytte, Sw. hydda; and F. hutte, of G. origin; all akin to E. hide to conceal. See Hude to conceal.

hutch.etymology: OE. hucche, huche, hoche, F. huche, LL. hutica.

hyacinth.etymology: L. hyacinthus a kind of flower, prob. the iris, gladiolus, or larkspur, also a kind of gem, perh. the sapphire; as, a proper name, Hyacinthus, a beautiful Laconian youth, beloved by Apollo, fr. Gr. hyacinthe. Cf. Jacinth. The hyacinth was fabled to have sprung from the blood of Hyacinthus, who was accidentally slain by Apollo.

hybrid.etymology: L. hybrida, hibrida, prob. allied to Gr. over: cf. F. hybride.

hydra.etymology: L. hydra, Gr. "y`dra; akin to "y`dwr water. See Otter the animal, Water.

hyssop.etymology: OE. hysope, ysope, OF. ysope, F. hysope, hyssope, L. hysopum, hyssopum, hyssopus, Gr. esov.

hysteria.etymology: NL.: cf. F. hystérie. See Hysteric.
